title: Shortages and Surpluses
objective: After this level you can explain what happens when prices are held too low or too high.
summary: A price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus, like Europe's butter mountains. A price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage, like rent control.

cards.headline: In the 1980s, Europe had a butter mountain. And a wine lake.
cards.body: Those were the nicknames for giant stored surpluses of butter and wine. They grew out of a rule that stopped prices doing Level 44's job.

cards.headline: Floors make surpluses
cards.body: Governments sometimes regulate prices by law. A price floor is the lowest price anyone may legally pay. Set it above the equilibrium price and sellers offer more than buyers want: a surplus. Level 44's cure, cutting the price, is now against the rules. So the extra has nowhere to go.

cards.fact: Europe's farm policy held prices high, and farmers produced more and more.
cards.context: When the Common Agricultural Policy began in 1962, it supported farmers mainly by keeping their prices artificially high. That's a floor, and Level 42 predicts the rest: a higher price, more supply. By the 1980s, the result was huge stored surpluses of butter and wine. (The wine was actually industrial alcohol. No lake of fine vintage, sadly.)

cards.headline: Ceilings make shortages
cards.body: Now flip it. A price ceiling is the highest price anyone may legally charge, often set to keep necessities affordable. Set it below equilibrium and buyers want more than sellers offer: a shortage. This time the price can't rise to close the gap, so the shortage stays. Rent control is the classic case: it can leave fewer apartments to rent than there would be at market rates.

mascot.line: Floors and ceilings get swapped all the time. A floor above equilibrium makes a surplus; a ceiling below, a shortage.

cards.headline: Price controls: tested
learned: A floor above equilibrium makes a surplus
Europe's butter mountains came from a floor
A ceiling below equilibrium makes a shortage
Rent control is the classic ceiling

options.label: The lowest price anyone may legally pay
The price where supply meets demand
The highest price anyone may legally charge
A tax added on top of a price
options.rationale: A ceiling caps the price; it adds nothing.

questions.explanation: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price, often meant to keep necessities affordable.

questions.prompt: Why did Europe's farm policy end up with butter mountains?

options.label: Prices held high made farmers produce more than buyers wanted
A bad harvest made farmers store butter for later
options.rationale: The surpluses came from too much production, not too little.

options.label: People in the 1980s stopped eating butter
options.rationale: The cause was the price policy, not a change in taste.

options.label: Prices were held so low that nobody would sell
options.rationale: Low prices would cause a shortage, not a surplus.

questions.explanation: Artificially high prices acted as a floor: farmers produced more and more, and the surplus had to be stored.

questions.prompt: From Level 44: in a free market, a shortage pushes the price up. What does a price ceiling below equilibrium do to that?

options.label: It speeds the rise up
options.rationale: A ceiling caps the price, so it cannot rise past it.

options.label: It turns the shortage into a surplus
options.rationale: Only a price held too high makes a surplus.

options.label: It has no effect on the shortage
options.rationale: It matters a lot: it stops the fix from happening.

options.label: It blocks the rise, so the shortage stays

questions.explanation: Normally sellers raise prices in a shortage. A ceiling forbids that, so the gap between wanted and offered doesn't close.
